title: Device never gets connected again after heartbeat timed out
body:
When heartbeats time out of a connected `Device`, the `Device` gets disconnected and never connected again. So both `is_connected()` (with only one device) and `is_connected(uuid)` (with uuid of previously connected device) never return true again. This also affects at least the `Device` thread update rate (100ms instead of 10ms).

Looking at the `device_impl` code, ` set_disconnected()` resets `_target_uuid_initialized`, but not `_target_uuid`. Now autopilot version is not requested again in `process_heartbeat()`, because `_target_uuid` was previously set to a nonzero value. Target uuid is never initialized and `Device` never gets connected again.

Fixes I tried, both work for me:

- `set_disconnected()` resets `_target_uuid_initialized`, `_target_uuid` and `_target_uuid_retries`.

-  `set_disconnected()` just doesn't reset  `_target_uuid_initialized`, keep the uuid of the prevously connected device (an obtained uuid never changes in my application, this might not work for others).

comments.body: @fklabach When testing your fix I realized that I could not actually reproduce the problem that you see. Does your vehicle actually send a UUID? Or does it send 0? When I test it with PX4 SITL it seems to reconnect just fine.

I use PX4 SITL too (with Gazebo) and it sends a nonzero uuid.
Does your SITL send autopilot version at regular intervals? For me, autopilot version is only sent when requested.
Once `_target_uuid` was set nonzero, autopilot version is never requested again in `process_heartbest()`.
To get connected again would require `process_autopilot_version()` to set `_target_uuid_initialized`. This never happens when we  don't request and receive the autopilot version.
Ok I think I understand, thanks.

title: Maintain a connection instance per component in case of UDP
body:
Right now we've maintain one connection per System (one or more components).
This creates problem if there are more than one component in a system.

Consider below scenario:

- After we receive heartbeat from a component A of a system on udp port (say, 14540), we fill source ip/port details as part of connection instance. When we receive heartbeat from another component B of the same system, **_Core assumes System IP may be changed due to Wifi disconnection._**
- While we're sending commands/messages, we need to make sure we send to IP/Port of the corresponding component whom it is meant to be.

I think, to support multi-component in core, we shall have one connection per component. We should map each component with its connection to make this happen.

Please provide better suggestions, if any.
It is linked to #304 . And hopefully the fix should be part of #310 .

title: Decide how to pass callbacks to API
body:
I see that we have inconsistency in the way callbacks are passed into the C++ API.

Some of the APIs use pass-by-value:
```
void subscribe_plugin_something(const subscribe_plugin_something_callback_t callback);
```

Others use pass-by-reference:
```
void subscribe_plugin_something(const subscribe_plugin_something_callback_t &callback);
```

From my understanding, pass-by-value leads to a copy (shallow or deep?) of the function object and therefore adds overhead, however, it prevents the case where the passed callback goes out of scope which can lead to a segfault.

@shakthi-prashanth-m @JonasVautherin opinions?

comments.body:
>passed callback goes out of scope which can lead to a segfault.

I dont think this happens, because callback is simply pointer to a function which exists thought the execution of the application (unless it is being loaded dynamically using `dlopen`). IMO, pass by value is ok.

I would pass by value as well. I found [this answer](https://stackoverflow.com/a/18366273/1368342) very interesting, including:

> That store makes passing by value more optimal. If there is any possibility you are storing a copy of the std::function, pass by value. Otherwise, either way is roughly equivalent: the only downside to by-value is if you are taking the same bulky std::function and having one sub method after another use it. Barring that, a move will be as efficient as a const&.
Do we have to use `std::move` anywhere or does that happen automatically?
From what I understand, it happens automatically. Otherwise it would really not be practical...
This has changed in the meantime anyway, and it seems to work well enough.

@julianoes 
ok, will check again.

Anyway, I would still appreciate if someone could explain what `does_support_mission_int()` means.
I sometimes get it with px4 SITL as well - not only with the H520.

Searching for it (https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/search?q=does_support_mission_int&unscoped_q=does_support_mission_int) does not give many clues and honestly makes the codebase here a bit difficult to approach.

Ok MAVSDK needs to receive the message [AUTOPILOT_VERSION](https://mavlink.io/en/messages/common.html#AUTOPILOT_VERSION) once because it needs to know about the `capabilities` flags.
One of those flags is [MAV_PROTOCOL_CAPABILITY_MISSION_INT](https://mavlink.io/en/messages/common.html#MAV_PROTOCOL_CAPABILITY_MISSION_INT).

This flag means that the vehicle supports the `_INT` version of the [mission protocol](https://mavlink.io/en/services/mission.html) which has better accuracy than the legacy one.

The fact that you get the `does_support_mission_int() = false` is because you have not received the `AUTOPILOT_VERION` message indicating the capabilities but does not actually mean that `_INT` messages are not allowed. Therefore, I've been trying to fix the problem of not receiving `AUTOPILOT_VERSION` instead of removing the check for mission int which is just a symptom but not the root cause!

title: Timesync adjusting outgoing message timestamps
body:
The usual method for timesync with mavlink is that outgoing messages are sent with the sender's clock source, and the receiver should translate it into their own time frame. However, we've seen now with MAVSDK that after an initial timesync exchange it adjusts the clock source for _outgoing_ messages. This causes massive confusion on the flight controller side, since it was trying to adjust timestamps on incoming messages to what the clock source on MAVSDK was _before_ it did the timesync. This might be the root cause of #960 ? It can also cause instability in both timesync algorithms since they try to estimate each other when the offset is constantly changing, instead of estimating a single offset which should be mostly constant.

To fix this, outgoing messages should be timestamped with a consistent clock source (preferably CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW, ie something that isn't affected by time jumps or temporary clock slewing on the host system), and only incoming messages should be adjusted via the timesync message.

FYI @irsdkv , @JonasVautherin suggested I tag you since you contributed this. Do you see any problems here? Would you have time to fix this?

Thanks @DanielePettenuzzo for the investigation.

comments.body:
In our case (using Autopilot time in MoCap system messages) we have not any problems with that so I can't say anything more related to that.

I can be wrong, but in my mind current MAVSDK tymesync mechanism (https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/pull/890) shouldn't cause these problems. Similar behavior [implemented in ROS](https://github.com/mavlink/mavros/blob/master/mavros/src/plugins/sys_time.cpp).

UPD. 
Unfortunately now I haven't much time to figure it out so I can just try to help, sorry.

Reading through your PR I don't see a problem there, everything looks good. However it looks like it has been changed since then: https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/8afd4640cebf4fae242a9ff9650d354cebab2f48/src/core/timesync.cpp#L42
It now responds with the offset from autopilot time, not system time, which is exactly the problem we now see on flight control side.

> it has been changed since then:

Yes it is related to https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/pull/934

More about this solution:

1. Source:
https://github.com/mavlink/mavros/blob/master/mavros/src/plugins/sys_time.cpp#L310

2. I think it can be a bad solution if `ros::Time::now()` is a host-machine time, not local adjusted clocks.

So I can understand that it might be a problem if we want to have MAVSDK at the same time as MAVROS running, because each of these is only designed to sync with a single external source.

What #934 does breaks the assumption of the timesync module in the Firmware, that the MAVSDK clock has constant offset, since Firmware sends at 10Hz, so gets responses and estimates the MAVSDK time offset before the MAVSDK has the firmware offset and shifts the clock in the first big step.

Perhaps one way (it feels a bit hacky) is to not respond to external timesync messages until the first timesync has completed with the autopilot. So [this line ](https://github.com/mavlink/MAVSDK/blob/8afd4640cebf4fae242a9ff9650d354cebab2f48/src/core/timesync.cpp#L45) needs to have something like `&& timesync_set` which is set true when the autopilot time is actually updated.

The 'proper' solution, a lot more work, is to fix the MAVSDK/Firmware/MAVROS to have multiple timesync offsets, based on component ID.
